description.from:
Adopt the best retrieval and knowledge-representation techniques from two external sources into the Papyrus knowledge-query engine, without violating our cost model.

**Sources**:
1. Cerebras Engineering, "How We Built Our Knowledge Base" (Tai, Kim, Gao, July 2026) — https://www.cerebras.ai/blog/how-we-built-our-knowledge-base. Production system, 15,000+ queries/day.
2. "Graph Engineering: 4 Models to 4 Prompts" (Boris Cherny, Full Course From Scratch, July 2026) — independently compiled from Anthropic's Knowledge Graph Cookbook, Building Effective AI Agents, and Claude API docs; **not an Anthropic publication and not endorsed by Anthropic**. Demonstration corpus is six Wikipedia articles, so treat its techniques as sound and its numbers as illustrative.

**Full design doc**: `docs/knowledge-retrieval-roadmap.md` — per-idea integration designs with verified file:line references, dependency graph, rejected-alternatives analysis. Background on the current retrieval path: `docs/internal-knowledge-research.md`.

## The two sources solve different layers

**Cerebras is retrieval-centric**: how do I FIND the right thing in a large pile? Unit of work is the document/chunk; answers are grounded in passages; the architecture compensates for any single scorer's weakness by running several retrievers and fusing their ranked lists (RRF, k=60), then reranking. Their core lesson — never trust a single retrieval technique — is the one Papyrus has not absorbed.

**The graph note is representation-centric**: how do I REPRESENT what a document says? Unit of work is the entity and the triple; answers are grounded in edges with citations. Its argument is that four separately-trained NLP systems (NER, relation classifier, entity resolver, summarizer) collapse into four LLM prompts, because a schema now does the work labeled training data used to.

They compose rather than compete, and they inform different epics here. Notably, graph traversal has a cold-start problem the note does not address — traversal needs a seed entity, and search is how you find one — which is further evidence they are layers, not alternatives.

## Where Papyrus stands

**Already as good or better than Cerebras**: curation gating (only human-accepted references become evidence — they have nothing like this, and it doubles as our cost governor), knowledge-graph expansion, quality-aware ranking profiles, token-budgeted context packs per consumer profile, versioned knowledge lineage.

**We already have the graph the note describes building.** `SemanticNode` (nodeKey, aliases, authorityScore), `SemanticRelation` with typed predicates including `mentions`, and query-time graph expansion are all in place. What we lack is a construction pipeline that populates it densely — which is exactly what the note is a recipe for.

**The retrieval gap**: Papyrus retrieval is embedding-only (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small → AWS S3 Vectors, 1536-dim cosine). For a threat-intelligence publication this is the worst possible single-retriever weakness: CVE IDs, file hashes, actor aliases, domains, and ATT&CK IDs are exactly the exact-token queries embeddings blur. There is also no recency signal (dates are not even in vector metadata), no rank fusion, no rerank, no contextual chunk prefixes, no signal gating on what enters the index — plus two latent defects: passage scoring carries hardcoded boosts tuned for a prior AI/ML-research corpus, and an 8-chunk cap means only the first ~1,440 words of long reports are semantically searchable.

**And we cannot currently measure any of it.** No golden queries, no baseline, no way to tell an improvement from a regression. That is why the eval epic goes first.

## Why architecture before volume

Ingestion has been deliberately throttled: importing a large corpus and then
needing to re-import it after an architecture change would be painful. Being
precise about what that fear covers tells us what actually has to be right
before scaling.

**Safely re-derivable from what we already store** — chunking, embedding model,
distillation artifacts, entity extraction, entity resolution, contextual
prefixes, and the entire vector index. All of these regenerate from the
`extracted_text` attachments plus the GraphQL records. No re-import, ever.

**NOT re-derivable** — anything needing the original fetched artifact. Today raw
bytes are archived only for PDFs (`_reference_source_attachment_record` is gated
on `_looks_like_pdf_uri` / `is_pdf_source` at `reference_url_text.py:166` and
`:257`), so accepted HTML references keep extracted text and nothing else. If we
later want tables, figures, layout, or simply better extraction, we must
re-fetch — and threat-intel sources get pulled, revised, and paywalled.

That single gap, not the retrieval architecture, is what genuinely gates safe
ingestion growth. It is why link-rot archival is P0 alongside the eval harness.

## Architectural decisions (current)

### AD-1: Graph traversal is a RETRIEVER, not a separate answering mode

When graph-grounded retrieval matures it contributes a ranked list fused (RRF) alongside semantic and lexical lists. It does NOT become a second query pipeline with its own LLM call and output shape.

Why: the engine ALREADY blends graph signal into one ranked list via hand-tuned constants in `_rank_structured_records` (`engine.py:2161-2180`: 1.0 anchors, 0.9 semantic-match-that-is-also-a-graph-neighbor, 0.6 shares-context-metadata, 0.8 expanded objects). Fusion is continuous with existing architecture; a separate mode would be genuinely new. RRF REPLACES those arbitrary constants with a principled rank-consensus score — it deletes heuristics rather than adding machinery. A separate mode would also require a query-time LLM call, breaking the "engine is LLM-free at query time" property we deliberately protect (only rerank may violate it, feature-flagged), plus query entity-linking to find seed nodes — whereas under fusion the seeds come free from semantic/lexical hits, which is already how `_expand_semantic_seed_matches` works.

**Consequence**: `fuse_ranked_lists()` MUST accept N ranked lists with per-list weights from day one. Do not hardcode two arms.

### AD-2: Entity extraction augments retrieval; it never gates it (v1)

Entity metadata BOOSTS and JOINS results; it is not a restrictive filter in v1. Extraction recall is unmeasured, and incomplete metadata used as an exclusion filter silently hides references the extractor missed — with total confidence. Restrictive filtering only after recall is measured and spot-checked.

### AD-3: Entity merges need a curation gate

Resolution errors are EDITORIAL errors, not retrieval-quality errors. Merging two distinct threat actors makes the publication issue false attribution claims laundered through our own citation machinery — a correction-worthy mistake, and the worst kind, because it looks well-sourced. Merges land as proposals requiring human confirmation before becoming canonical, mirroring the accepted-reference gate. Un-merging must stay cheap.

### AD-4: Retrieval-changing epics land serially, not in parallel

The scoring cleanup, hybrid lexical, and age-decay epics all touch `engine.py` and `ranking.py` within lines of each other. Concurrent dispatch produces merge conflicts at best and semantic conflicts at worst (two epics both renormalizing ranking weights). Land one at a time; re-verify line references after each merge.

## The epics

**Phase 0 — make growth safe, and make change measurable**
1. **Archive raw source bytes for all accepted references** (P0) — link-rot
   insurance; the real precondition for scaling ingestion.
2. **Retrieval eval harness** (P0) — golden query set from the real corpus,
   hit@k/MRR, baseline captured and committed before anything else lands.

**Phase 1 — subtract, then add cheaply**
3. **Delete dead ranking config** (P1) — nothing ever sets `ranking.profile` or
   `ranking.diversity`; ~27 constants exist and one path has ever run. Net
   negative diff, and it simplifies the code the next epics touch.
4. **Passage-scoring cleanup** (P1) — retire the prior corpus's boosts, extend
   heading boosts for threat-intel structure, fix the token regex.
5. **Hybrid lexical (BM25) + RRF fusion** (P1) — the anchor investment, and the
   lossless safety net under every lossy transformation that follows.
6. **Age decay** (P2) — recency as a tie-breaker.

**Phase 2 — representation (shares one rebuild)**
7. **Reference entity extraction** (P2) — normalized artifacts with grounded
   per-entity descriptions; entity metadata additive-only per AD-2.
8. **Entity resolution + graph promotion** (P3) — canonical nodes and aliases
   into the existing graph, curation-gated per AD-3, with hard cost guards.
9. **Contextual chunks + gating** (P3) — document context in embeddings, lift
   the 8-chunk cap.

**Phase 3 — discovery and surfaces**
10. **Exploratory research budget** (P3) — deliberately research adjacent,
    unsteered territory. Everything else in this initiative narrows focus; this
    is the counterweight that lets the system surprise its operators.
11. **Named scope bundles** (P4, deferred) — YAGNI at current corpus size, and
    in tension with item 10.
12. **MCP retrieval primitives** (P4, deferred) — useful, not load-bearing.
13. **Eval-gated rerank** (P4) — the only recurring per-query LLM cost; ships
    only if the eval proves a win.

Plus a **rebuild-coordination chore**, because batching index rebuilds is an
instruction to people spread across three briefs.

## What we are deliberately NOT copying

Ingest-everything (our curation gate stays), Socket-Mode real-time ingestion (our cadence is editorial), per-user defaults (ours are per-desk/procedure), a separate graph answering pipeline (AD-1), and every piece of always-on infrastructure Cerebras's enterprise scale amortizes.

## Hard constraints (non-negotiable)

1. **Scale to zero.** No provisioned-capacity services, no always-on components, no fixed monthly floors. Everything pay-per-use. This is why OpenSearch is disqualified (~$350/month floor × N instances).
2. **Fleet of single-publication instances, NOT multi-tenant.** Each Papyrus installation is one publication with its own stack. Never introduce tenant awareness. The economics: many instances run simultaneously, almost all idle.
3. **The knowledge-query Lambda is stdlib-only.** `amplify/functions/knowledge-query/resource.ts` bundles by copying `src/papyrus_knowledge_query` verbatim with an intentionally empty requirements.txt. Python 3.12, ARM64, 512 MB. No new pip dependencies in anything the Lambda imports.

## Sequencing and rebuild coupling

Eval harness first. Then the phase-1 epics serially (AD-4). Phase 2 shares ONE full corpus re-embed — do not rebuild after extraction and again after contextual chunks. Age-decay's metadata addition is backward-compatible and may ride along with any convenient sync. See the rebuild-coordination task for trigger conditions and procedure.

## For implementers

- **This plan is not frozen.** It records current decisions and their reasoning
  so nobody re-derives them from scratch. Model capability moves quickly and we
  intend to re-examine this as it does — challenge any decision here if you have
  information we did not.
- Verify every file:line reference before editing — they were verified 2026-07-19 and drift as epics merge.
- Tests live in `procedures/newsroom/tests/` (see `test_knowledge_query.py`). Add tests with every change.
- Local smoke: `PYTHONPATH=src python -m papyrus_newsroom knowledge-query --query "..." --format structured --execution local` (see docs/internal-knowledge-research.md for CLI usage and env vars).
- Report before/after golden-set numbers on any retrieval-changing PR.
- Repo-visible content constraint: keep examples generic (CVE IDs, hashes, domains); no ransomware/exfiltration/key-leak themed examples.
description.to:
Get the Papyrus knowledge base to a state where the corpus can grow confidently, retrieval works on this domain, and the system surfaces things its operators did not think to ask for — without breaking the cost model or the editorial guarantees.

**Full design doc**: `docs/knowledge-retrieval-roadmap.md`. Architecture orientation: `project/wiki/knowledge-base-architecture.md`. Current retrieval path: `docs/internal-knowledge-research.md`.

## The goal

Papyrus is meant to be **steered, not operated**. That implies a knowledge base that covers ground the operator did not individually specify, sources everything it claims, and does not require a human to shepherd each document through by hand. We are not there. Getting there needs four things that are currently missing or weak: sources we cannot lose, a way to tell whether a change helped, retrieval that handles this domain's exact identifiers and freshness, and a discovery mechanism that is not purely reactive.

## What is actually constraining us

Three constraints, in the order they bite.

**1. Curation throughput.** Every accepted reference passes through one human. The corpus is small because of that gate. It is also the gate that makes citations trustworthy and keeps per-document LLM spend bounded, so it stays — but almost everything else in this initiative improves machinery *downstream* of it. Assisted triage (automating around the decision without automating the decision) is therefore the highest-leverage single epic here, and it is easy to overlook precisely because it is not a retrieval problem.

**2. Source durability.** Ingestion has been deliberately throttled out of a concern that a large import would need re-importing after an architecture change. Being precise about that concern is clarifying:

- *Safely re-derivable from what we already store*: chunking, embedding model, distillation artifacts, entity extraction, entity resolution, contextual prefixes, the entire vector index. All regenerate from `extracted_text` attachments plus the GraphQL records. No re-import, ever.
- *NOT re-derivable*: anything needing the original fetched artifact. Raw bytes are archived only for PDFs today (`_reference_source_attachment_record` is gated on `_looks_like_pdf_uri` / `is_pdf_source` at `reference_url_text.py:166` and `:257`), so accepted HTML references keep extracted text and nothing else. Threat-intel sources get revised, pulled, and paywalled.

That single gap — not the retrieval architecture — is what genuinely gates safe corpus growth.

**3. Retrieval quality.** Retrieval is embedding-only (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small → S3 Vectors, 1536-dim cosine). For a threat-intelligence publication this is the worst available single-retriever weakness: CVE IDs, hashes, actor aliases, domains, and ATT&CK IDs are exact-token queries that embeddings blur. There is no recency signal (dates are not even in vector metadata), no rank fusion, and no rerank — plus two latent defects: passage scoring carries hardcoded boosts tuned for a prior AI/ML-research corpus, and an 8-chunk cap means only the first ~1,440 words of long reports are searchable. And none of it is measurable today.

## Where the ideas came from

Two external sources informed the technical approach. They are inputs, not the organizing principle.

1. Cerebras Engineering, "How We Built Our Knowledge Base" (Tai, Kim, Gao, July 2026) — https://www.cerebras.ai/blog/how-we-built-our-knowledge-base. Production system, 15,000+ queries/day. **Retrieval-centric**: how do I find the right thing? Core lesson — never trust a single retrieval technique; run several and fuse the ranked lists.
2. "Graph Engineering: 4 Models to 4 Prompts" (Boris Cherny, Full Course From Scratch, July 2026) — independently compiled from Anthropic's Knowledge Graph Cookbook and related docs; **not an Anthropic publication and not endorsed by Anthropic**, demonstration corpus is six Wikipedia articles, so treat its techniques as sound and its numbers as illustrative. **Representation-centric**: how do I represent what a document says? Its most transferable idea is that a grounded one-line entity description written during extraction is what makes later resolution possible.

They compose rather than compete. Note that graph traversal has a cold-start problem the second source does not address — traversal needs a seed entity, and search is how you find one.

What Papyrus already does as well or better than either: curation gating, knowledge-graph expansion, quality-aware ranking, token-budgeted context packs, versioned lineage. We already have the graph the second source describes building; what we lack is a pipeline that populates it densely.

## Sequencing

Five phases. The ordering reflects three rules: unblock the bottleneck before adding load to it, subtract before adding, and do not build machinery whose value scales with corpus size while the corpus is small.

**Phase A — Foundations. Run in parallel; nothing else should start first.**
- *Archive raw source bytes* (P0) — link-rot insurance; the real precondition for growth.
- *Retrieval eval harness* (P0) — golden queries, baseline captured and committed before any ranking change.

These touch entirely different files (ingestion vs. new test infrastructure) and can proceed simultaneously without conflict. Both gate what follows.

**Phase B — Subtract, then sharpen. Strictly serial (AD-4).**
- *Delete dead ranking config* (P1) — net negative diff; simplifies the exact code the next items modify. First, because everything after is easier in the smaller codebase.
- *Passage-scoring cleanup* (P1) — small, self-contained, fixes a demonstrable defect. Good contractor calibration.
- *Hybrid lexical + RRF fusion* (P1) — the anchor investment and the lossless safety net under every lossy transformation that follows.
- *Age decay* (P2) — recency as tie-breaker.

All four touch `engine.py` / `ranking.py` within lines of each other. Land one at a time and re-verify line references after each merge.

**Phase C — Unblock the bottleneck, then grow.**
- *Assisted curation triage* (P1) — the constraint. Independent of all retrieval work; could technically start during Phase A, and should if there is capacity.
- *Exploratory research budget* (P3) — blocked by triage, because adding review volume to a saturated bottleneck makes things worse.

This is where the corpus actually starts growing, which is why it precedes the representation work.

**Phase D — Representation, once there is material to represent.**
- *Reference entity extraction* (P2) — grounded per-entity descriptions; metadata additive-only (AD-2).
- *Contextual chunks + gating* (P3) — needs the lexical DF table from Phase B and extraction from this phase.
- *Coordinate vector index rebuilds* (chore) — ONE re-embed covering extraction and contextual chunks.
- *Entity resolution + graph promotion* (P3) — last in this phase and deliberately so: highest blast radius (AD-3), and its value is proportional to alias fragmentation, which barely exists at a few hundred references.

**Why representation comes after growth**: entity resolution built against a small corpus is built against a corpus too small to validate it — few actors appear under multiple names yet, so the failure modes that matter would not surface until later anyway. Extraction is closer to a judgment call and could move earlier if there is a concrete pull for it; resolution should not.

**Phase E — Optional and deferred.**
- *MCP retrieval primitives* (P4) — useful, not load-bearing; agents already reach retrieval via the Tactus harness.
- *Named scope bundles* (P4) — YAGNI at current corpus size, and in tension with exploratory research.
- *Eval-gated rerank* (P4) — the only recurring per-query LLM cost; ships only if the eval proves a win, and "it does not" is a success outcome worth the measurement.

## Architectural decisions (current)

### AD-1: Graph traversal is a RETRIEVER, not a separate answering mode

When graph-grounded retrieval matures it contributes a ranked list fused (RRF) alongside semantic and lexical lists — not a second query pipeline with its own LLM call.

Why: the engine ALREADY blends graph signal into one ranked list via hand-tuned constants in `_rank_structured_records` (`engine.py:2161-2180`). Fusion is continuous with existing architecture; RRF replaces those arbitrary constants with a principled rank-consensus score, deleting heuristics rather than adding machinery. A separate mode would require a query-time LLM call, breaking the LLM-free-at-query-time property we protect everywhere except the feature-flagged reranker, plus query entity-linking to find seeds — whereas under fusion the seeds come free from semantic/lexical hits.

**Consequence**: `fuse_ranked_lists()` MUST accept N ranked lists with per-list weights from day one.

### AD-2: Entity metadata augments retrieval; it never gates it (v1)

Entity metadata boosts and joins; it is not a restrictive filter until extraction recall is measured. Incomplete metadata used as an exclusion filter silently hides material with total confidence. The dangerous failure of extraction is omission, not hallucination.

### AD-3: Entity merges need a curation gate

Resolution errors are EDITORIAL errors. Merging two distinct threat actors makes the publication issue false attribution claims laundered through its own citation machinery. Merges land as proposals requiring human confirmation; un-merging stays cheap.

### AD-4: Retrieval-changing epics land serially, not in parallel

Phase B's four epics touch the same files within lines of each other. Concurrent dispatch produces merge conflicts at best and semantic conflicts at worst.

## Hard constraints (non-negotiable)

1. **Scale to zero.** No provisioned-capacity services, no always-on components, no fixed monthly floors. This is why OpenSearch is disqualified (~$350/month floor × N instances).
2. **Fleet of single-publication instances, NOT multi-tenant.** Each installation is one publication with its own stack. Never introduce tenant awareness.
3. **The knowledge-query Lambda is stdlib-only.** It bundles by copying `src/papyrus_knowledge_query` verbatim with an intentionally empty requirements.txt. Python 3.12, ARM64, 512 MB.
4. **The curation gate stays.** Automate around the human decision, never the decision itself. No confidence score may become an auto-accept threshold.

## For implementers

- **This plan is not frozen.** It records current decisions and their reasoning so nobody re-derives them from scratch. Model capability moves quickly and we intend to re-examine this as it does — challenge any decision here if you have information we did not.
- Verify every file:line reference before editing — they were verified 2026-07-25 and drift as epics merge.
- Tests live in `procedures/newsroom/tests/` (see `test_knowledge_query.py`). Add tests with every change.
- Local smoke: `PYTHONPATH=src python -m papyrus_newsroom knowledge-query --query "..." --format structured --execution local`.
- Report before/after golden-set numbers on any retrieval-changing PR — as a regression tripwire, not a score to maximize.
- Work through the Kanbus CLI; do not edit `project/` JSON directly (`CONTRIBUTING_AGENT.template.md`). Wiki markdown under `project/wiki/` may be edited directly.
- Repo-visible content constraint: keep examples generic (CVE IDs, hashes, domains).
